subject: math
description: Students compute the dot product of two vectors in component form, $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}=u_1v_1+u_2v_2$ (and its $3$D extension $u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3$). They use the relationship $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}=\|\vec{u}\|\,\|\vec{v}\|\cos\theta$ to find the angle between two vectors, determine whether two vectors are orthogonal by testing $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}=0$, and compute the scalar and vector projection of one vector onto another using $\operatorname{proj}_{\vec{v}}\vec{u}=\dfrac{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}}{\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}}\,\vec{v}$. Answers are given exactly with radicals, $\pi$, and fractions rather than rounded decimals unless an approximation is requested.
subSkills: Compute the dot product of two vectors given in component form ($2$D and $3$D)
Use $\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}=\|\vec{v}\|^2$ to relate the dot product to magnitude
Find the angle between two vectors via $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}}{\|\vec{u}\|\,\|\vec{v}\|}$
Decompose a vector into components parallel and orthogonal to a given vector
Solve for an unknown component that makes two vectors orthogonal or parallel
Apply the dot product to work ($W=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{d}$) and geometric contexts

problemArchetypes.name: Angle between vectors (exact special angle)
problemArchetypes.example: Find the angle between $\vec{u}=\langle 1,\sqrt{3}\rangle$ and $\vec{v}=\langle \sqrt{3},1\rangle$. (Answer: $\cos\theta=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{4}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Angle between vectors (general, approximate)
problemArchetypes.example: Find the angle between $\vec{u}=\langle 2,3\rangle$ and $\vec{v}=\langle -1,4\rangle$ to the nearest degree. (Answer: $\cos\theta=\frac{10}{\sqrt{13}\,\sqrt{17}}$, so $\theta\approx 47.7^\circ$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Solve for an unknown component
problemArchetypes.example: Find $k$ so that $\vec{u}=\langle k,5\rangle$ and $\vec{v}=\langle 2,-3\rangle$ are orthogonal. (Answer: $2k-15=0\Rightarrow k=\frac{15}{2}$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Scalar projection (component)
problemArchetypes.example: Find the scalar projection of $\vec{u}=\langle 4,3\rangle$ onto $\vec{v}=\langle 1,0\rangle$. (Answer: $\operatorname{comp}_{\vec{v}}\vec{u}=\frac{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}}{\|\vec{v}\|}=4$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Orthogonal decomposition
problemArchetypes.example: Write $\vec{u}=\langle 5,2\rangle$ as the sum of a vector parallel to $\vec{v}=\langle 1,1\rangle$ and a vector orthogonal to $\vec{v}$. (Answer: $\vec{u}=\langle \frac{7}{2},\frac{7}{2}\rangle+\langle \frac{3}{2},-\frac{3}{2}\rangle$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Work done by a force
problemArchetypes.example: A constant force $\vec{F}=\langle 6,2\rangle$ moves an object along displacement $\vec{d}=\langle 4,1\rangle$. Find the work. (Answer: $W=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{d}=24+2=26$.)

Easy.description: Single-step computation with small integer components. Compute a dot product directly, or test orthogonality by checking if the dot product is zero. No magnitudes or radicals required.
constraints: Vectors are 2D with integer components, each $|\,\text{component}\,|\le 6$
Task is one operation: a dot product, or an orthogonality yes/no test
No square roots, fractions, or inverse trig in the answer
Angle questions, if any, use perpendicular ($\frac{\pi}{2}$) or parallel detection only

Medium.description: Two to three steps involving magnitudes and the angle or projection formulas, where the result is an exact special-angle value or a clean fraction. Includes solving for an unknown component for orthogonality and computing vector projections.
constraints: Requires computing one or two magnitudes with radicals (e.g. $\sqrt{5},\sqrt{13}$)
Angle answers are exact unit-circle values such as $\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{3\pi}{4}$
Scalar or vector projections with fractional coefficients are allowed
Solving $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}=0$ for one unknown component is Medium

Hard.description: Multi-step problems that combine several operations, require orthogonal decomposition, use 3D vectors, yield non-special angles requiring $\cos^{-1}$ with an approximation, or are set in an applied/geometric context requiring setup before computation.
constraints: May require an orthogonal decomposition into parallel and perpendicular parts
May use 3D vectors or symbolic/parameterized components
Angle answers may be non-special, expressed exactly as $\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\dots}{\dots}\right)$ and approximated to the nearest degree
Applied context (work, geometry, proving a triangle is right) must be translated into vectors first

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Treats the dot product as a vector by multiplying componentwise instead of summing
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}=\langle u_1v_1,\,u_2v_2\rangle$ (e.g. $\langle 15,-8\rangle$) instead of the scalar $u_1v_1+u_2v_2=7$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Adds the components of each vector first, then multiplies, or otherwise mishandles signs
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Computes $(u_1+u_2)(v_1+v_2)$ or drops the negative sign, e.g. $3(5)+4(2)=23$ instead of $3(5)+(-4)(2)=7$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets to divide by the product of the magnitudes when finding the angle
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Sets $\cos\theta=\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}$ and takes $\cos^{-1}$ of an out-of-range value, or omits one magnitude in the denominator

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses the orthogonality condition with the parallel condition
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls vectors orthogonal when components are proportional ($\frac{u_1}{v_1}=\frac{u_2}{v_2}$) rather than when $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}=0$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Uses $\|\vec{v}\|$ instead of $\|\vec{v}\|^2$ (i.e. $\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}$) in the vector projection denominator
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Computes $\operatorname{proj}_{\vec{v}}\vec{u}=\frac{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}}{\|\vec{v}\|}\vec{v}$, scaling $\vec{v}$ by the scalar projection instead of $\frac{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}}{\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses the scalar projection (a number) with the vector projection (a vector)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Gives the scalar $\frac{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}}{\|\vec{v}\|}$ when a vector $\langle\,,\,\rangle$ is required, or vice versa

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets the magnitude square root, using $u_1^2+u_2^2$ as the magnitude
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Uses $\|\vec{u}\|=u_1^2+u_2^2$ instead of $\sqrt{u_1^2+u_2^2}$, producing the wrong $\cos\theta$ and angle

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Projects onto the wrong vector, swapping $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Computes $\operatorname{proj}_{\vec{u}}\vec{v}$ when $\operatorname{proj}_{\vec{v}}\vec{u}$ was asked, using $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{u}$ in the denominator
